title: ThSQCA
text: ThSQCA is an R package that reruns a QCA analysis across a range of thresholds, under identical settings, and records how the sufficiency solutions change. Truth table construction and minimization are delegated to the QCA package, so the computational core is the same as in a standard analysis.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
text: In part 2 we ran all four sweeps. Two questions remain for a careful analysis. First, QCA can produce three kinds of solution (complex, parsimonious, and intermediate); which should you use? Second, what if a cell has more than one minimal solution? This post answers both with a second, smaller practice data set.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
text:
A second practice data set
We simulate 60 business software accounts. Each has a renewal score (RNW) and three evaluations: trust (TRU), price (PRC), and support (SUP), all from 0 to 10. In this simulated world, renewal is high when trust is high and either price or support is high. The three evaluations are strongly correlated, which will leave some combinations of conditions unobserved. That is deliberate, because unobserved combinations are exactly what the three solution types treat differently.

library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)

Loading required package: admisc



To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.




Practice data set 2
make_demo_data2 <- function(n = 60, seed = 89, rho = 0.85) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  L   <- rnorm(n)
  mk  <- function() clip(6 + 2 * (rho * L + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)))
  TRU <- mk(); PRC <- mk(); SUP <- mk()
  RNW <- clip(pmin(TRU, pmax(PRC, SUP)) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(RNW, TRU, PRC, SUP)
}

demo2 <- make_demo_data2()
head(demo2)


  RNW TRU PRC SUP
1   3   3   4   4
2   6   8   7   7
3   9   9   9   7
4   5   5   4   6
5  10  10   8   9
6   1   2   4   5

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
text:
Unobserved combinations (“logical remainders”)
With three conditions, each either high or low, there are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 possible combinations. QCA lists them in a truth table. Let us build one by hand with the QCA package, using renewal of 5 or more as the outcome and 7 or more as “high” for each condition.

bin2 <- data.frame(
  RNW = as.integer(demo2$RNW >= 5),
  TRU = as.integer(demo2$TRU >= 7),
  PRC = as.integer(demo2$PRC >= 7),
  SUP = as.integer(demo2$SUP >= 7)
)

tt2 <- truthTable(bin2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
tt2


  OUT: output value
    n: number of cases in configuration
 incl: sufficiency inclusion score
  PRI: proportional reduction in inconsistency

    TRU PRC SUP   OUT    n   incl  PRI  
1    0   0   0     0     30  0.433 0.433
2    0   0   1     1     7   0.857 0.857
4    0   1   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
6    1   0   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
7    1   1   0     1     4   1.000 1.000
8    1   1   1     1     13  1.000 1.000


Look at the row numbers on the left. Only 6 of the 8 possible combinations appear (rows 3 and 5 are missing), because the data contain no accounts with, for example, high trust alone, or high price evaluation alone. The combinations that are missing are the logical remainders. The column n is the number of accounts in each combination, incl is how consistently they renew, and OUT is 1 when the combination is consistent enough to count as sufficient.
Remainders matter because Boolean minimization can use them to make a formula shorter, and the three solution types differ in whether, and how, they do that.









Solution type
Remainders used
include
dir.exp




Complex
none
"" (default)
NULL


Parsimonious
any remainder that shortens the formula
"?"
NULL


Intermediate
only remainders that agree with your stated expectations
"?"
e.g. c(1, 1, 1)



Here dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1) says: we expect high trust, high price evaluation, and high support each to favor renewal.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
section: The three solution types, side by side
text:
The three solution types, side by side
We run the same outcome threshold sweep (renewal of 5, 6, 7, and 8) three times, changing only the solution type.

thr2  <- c(TRU = 7, PRC = 7, SUP = 7)
cond2 <- c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP")

run2 <- function(...) {
  otSweep(dat = demo2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = cond2, sweep_range = 5:8,
          thrX = thr2, incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, ...)
}

res_cx <- run2()                                     # complex
res_ps <- run2(include = "?")                        # parsimonious

Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.

res_im <- run2(include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1))  # intermediate

data.frame(
  thrY         = 5:8,
  complex      = res_cx$summary$expression,
  parsimonious = res_ps$summary$expression,
  intermediate = res_im$summary$expression
)

  thrY            complex   parsimonious       intermediate
1    5      SUP + TRU*PRC      TRU + SUP      SUP + TRU*PRC
2    6 TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP TRU + ~PRC*SUP TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP
3    7            TRU*SUP        TRU*SUP            TRU*SUP
4    8        No solution    No solution        No solution


The warning shown with the output is a note from ThSQCA: at renewal of 5, the parsimonious analysis has more than one equally short solution. We come back to this below.
At renewal of 7, all three agree (TRU*SUP), and at 8 none finds a solution. At 5 and 6 the parsimonious solution is shorter. For example, at renewal of 5 it reports TRU + SUP, whereas the complex solution is SUP + TRU*PRC. The term TRU alone covers the combination “high trust, but low price and support evaluations”, which does not appear in the data. The parsimonious solution is willing to assume that this unobserved combination would also be sufficient. The complex solution makes no such assumption. In this particular data set the intermediate solution happens to coincide with the complex one.
How to choose:









Solution
When it is a good choice
Strength
Caution




Complex
Exploration; you want no assumptions about unobserved cases
Every claim rests on observed cases
Formulas can be long


Parsimonious
You want to see the maximal simplification
Shortest formulas
May rely on implausible remainders


Intermediate
Theory-driven reporting
Uses only plausible remainders
Needs a justified dir.exp



Whatever you choose, keep it the same across the whole sweep, and say which one you used.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
section: When a cell has more than one minimal solution
text:
When a cell has more than one minimal solution
Boolean minimization can return several equally short solutions for the same truth table. By default ThSQCA reports the first one (M1) and records the number of solutions in n_solutions. To see all of them, use extract_mode = "all".

res_all <- run2(include = "?", extract_mode = "all")

Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.

summary(res_all)

OTS Summary
=========== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: RNW 
  Conditions: TRU, PRC, SUP 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 thrY                   expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    5 M1: TRU + SUP; M2: PRC + SUP 0.967 0.690           2
    6           M1: TRU + ~PRC*SUP 0.963 0.788           1
    7                  M1: TRU*SUP 0.875 0.667           1
    8                  No solution    NA    NA           0

Note: 1 threshold setting(s) had multiple solutions.
      Use generate_report() for full details.


At renewal of 5, the parsimonious analysis finds two minimal solutions of equal length (multiple minimal solutions), TRU + SUP and PRC + SUP. Each of them relies on a different unobserved combination, which is why neither can be preferred on the data alone. ThSQCA prints a note when this happens.
If you prefer a compact view, use extract_mode = "essential". It separates the terms that are present in every solution from the rest.

res_ess <- run2(include = "?", extract_mode = "essential")

Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.

res_ess$summary[, c("thrY", "expression", "selective_terms",
                    "unique_terms", "n_solutions")]

  thrY     expression selective_terms   unique_terms n_solutions
1    5            SUP       TRU + PRC M1:TRU; M2:PRC           2
2    6 TRU + ~PRC*SUP            <NA>           <NA>           1
3    7        TRU*SUP            <NA>           <NA>           1
4    8    No solution            <NA>           <NA>           0





Term type
Meaning
Here (renewal of 5)




Essential
present in every solution
SUP


Selective
present in some solutions
TRU and PRC


Unique
present in only one solution
TRU in M1, PRC in M2



ThSQCA records the alternatives, but deciding which one to prioritize is a theoretical judgment that stays with the researcher.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
text: This is the first part of a beginner’s series on ThSQCA, an R package for threshold-sweep qualitative comparative analysis (QCA). You do not need to know QCA beforehand. By the end of this post you will have run a threshold sweep yourself and read its result.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
text:
The one idea you need
QCA looks for combinations of conditions that are sufficient for an outcome. Suppose we study customer loyalty. A combination such as “high quality AND high service” is sufficient for high loyalty if (almost) every customer who has both also has high loyalty.
To do this, QCA first has to decide who counts as “high”. With survey scores from 0 to 10, we pick a threshold: a customer is “high” on a variable when the score is greater than or equal to the threshold. In this series, each score is split at the threshold into “high” and “not high” (crisp-set QCA).
Here is the catch. A threshold of 7 and a threshold of 8 are both reasonable, but they can lead to different answers. A normal QCA analysis picks one threshold and reports one answer. ThSQCA reruns the same analysis for a whole range of thresholds and puts all the answers in one table, so you can see where the answer holds and where it changes.
ThSQCA does not replace the QCA package. For every threshold, it calls QCA’s truthTable() and minimize() for you, with identical settings each time, and collects the results.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
text:
Step 1: install the packages
Run this once. (If you already installed them, skip it.)

install.packages(c("QCA", "ThSQCA"))

Then load ThSQCA in every new R session:

library(ThSQCA)

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
section: Step 2: create a small practice data set
text:
Step 2: create a small practice data set
To keep things reproducible, we simulate 400 customers. Each has four scores from 0 to 10: loyalty (LOY), and evaluations of quality (QUA), service (SER), and store environment (ENV). In this simulated world, loyalty is high when quality and service are both high, or (a little less strongly) when quality and environment are both high. A good analysis should discover this.

make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()
head(demo)

  LOY QUA SER ENV
1   7   7   9   3
2   5   4   7   5
3   4   6   4   4
4   6   6   6   4
5   5   5   4   7
6   0   1   2   5


Each row is one customer. You do not have to understand the function above; it only produces the practice data. With your own data, you would simply read your file into a data frame with these kinds of columns.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
text:
Step 3: run the sweep
We want to know: how does the answer change as we raise the bar for “high loyalty”? So we keep the thresholds of the three conditions fixed at 7, and vary the outcome threshold from 5 to 8. This is called an outcome threshold sweep, and the function is otSweep().

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = demo,
  outcome     = "LOY",
  conditions  = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range = 5:8,
  thrX        = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7)
)

Here is what each line means.







Argument
Meaning




dat
the data frame to analyze


outcome
the outcome column


conditions
the condition columns


sweep_range
the outcome thresholds to try: here 5, 6, 7, and 8


thrX
the fixed threshold for each condition: “high” means 7 or more



Two settings are not written here because they have defaults: the minimum consistency for a combination to count as sufficient (incl.cut, default 0.8) and the minimum number of cases per combination (n.cut, default 1).

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
text:
Step 4: read the result

summary(res)

OTS Summary
=========== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: LOY 
  Conditions: QUA, SER, ENV 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 thrY        expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    5 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.981 0.403           1
    6 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.926 0.565           1
    7           QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
    8       No solution    NA    NA           0


The table has one row per outcome threshold. The columns are:

thrY: the outcome threshold used in that row. In the first row, “high loyalty” means LOY >= 5.
expression: the sufficient combination found. * means AND, + means OR, and ~ means NOT.
inclS: solution consistency. How reliably the cases covered by the solution are members of the outcome. Higher is better, and 1 is perfect.
covS: solution coverage. The share of the outcome cases that the solution explains.
n_solutions: how many minimal solutions were found (1 here).

Now read the expression column from top to bottom.

At LOY >= 5 and LOY >= 6, two combinations are sufficient: QUA*SER (high quality and high service) and QUA*ENV (high quality and a high store environment).
At LOY >= 7, only QUA*SER remains.
At LOY >= 8, the result is No solution. At this level, no combination of the three conditions reached the required consistency.

This is exactly what the simulation was built to contain, and it shows why a sweep is useful. Had we analyzed only LOY >= 6, we would have reported two paths. Had we analyzed only LOY >= 7, we would have reported one. The sweep shows that the answer depends on how high the target is, and where it stops working altogether.
A note on “No solution”: it is a technical result, not a statement that no route to high loyalty exists. It means that, for these data and these settings, QCA could not produce a minimal solution that meets the consistency requirement.

In the next part we will look more closely at the four kinds of sweeps (outcome, one condition, several conditions, and both together), and at how to choose the range of thresholds in a way you can defend.
The full package tutorial is available in the ThSQCA documentation, and the methodology is described in Toyoda (2026), Quality & Quantity.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
The basics list introduced the standard readings for learning QCA. The next question is probably “How is it actually used in research?” Here are papers from marketing and management that are worth reading as models for your own work, together with the theoretical background from management and organization research, grouped by purpose.
As in the basics list, the summaries stay within what the publishers’ abstracts say.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
1. Applications in marketing and services

Ordanini, A., Parasuraman, A., & Rubera, G. (2014). When the recipe is more important than the ingredients: A qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of service innovation configurations. Journal of Service Research, 17(2), 134-149. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094670513513337 Studies luxury hotel services and uses QCA to examine which combinations of attributes lead to the adoption of a new service. An application that looks not only at individual attributes but at how they are combined.
Frambach, R. T., Fiss, P. C., & Ingenbleek, P. T. M. (2016). How important is customer orientation for firm performance? A fuzzy set analysis of orientations, strategies, and environments. Journal of Business Research, 69(4), 1428-1436. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2015.10.120 Combines customer orientation with other strategic orientations, strategy types, and market environments, and uses fsQCA to find the configurations that go with high firm performance. An application that considers the role of customer orientation through its combinations with other conditions.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
section: 2. Theoretical background in management and organization research
text:
2. Theoretical background in management and organization research

Fiss, P. C. (2007). A set-theoretic approach to organizational configurations. Academy of Management Review, 32(4), 1180-1198. https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2007.26586092 Treats an organization as a combination of elements and argues for analyzing the link between those combinations and outcomes with set theory. A foundation for thinking about several combinations that lead to the same outcome.
Fiss, P. C. (2011). Building better causal theories: A fuzzy set approach to typologies in organization research. Academy of Management Journal, 54(2), 393-420. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.60263120 Analyzes organizational typologies with fuzzy sets and examines the combinations of conditions that lead to an outcome. Important for understanding that the causes can be asymmetric between the presence and the absence of an outcome.
Woodside, A. G. (2013). Moving beyond multiple regression analysis to algorithms: Calling for adoption of a paradigm shift from symmetric to asymmetric thinking in data analysis and crafting theory. Journal of Business Research, 66(4), 463-472. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2012.12.021 Alongside the effects of single variables in multiple regression, it proposes an analysis that looks at combinations of conditions and at causal asymmetry. It discusses how to analyze data and build theory, using regression and fsQCA on the same data.
Misangyi, V. F., Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., Crilly, D., & Aguilera, R. (2017). Embracing causal complexity: The emergence of a neo-configurational perspective. Journal of Management, 43(1), 255-282. https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206316679252 Reviews how QCA has developed in management and organization research and sets out a “neo-configurational perspective” for capturing causal complexity. It links set membership, necessity and sufficiency, and counterfactual analysis to theoretical viewpoints.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
section: 3. How to run and report an analysis (practical guides)
text:
3. How to run and report an analysis (practical guides)

Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., & Aguilera, R. V. (2018). Studying configurations with qualitative comparative analysis: Best practices in strategy and organization research. Strategic Organization, 16(4), 482-495. https://doi.org/10.1177/1476127018786487 Sets out practical guidelines for QCA in strategy and organization research. It covers the whole course of a study, from model building and case selection to calibration, analysis, reporting, and interpretation.
Pappas, I. O., & Woodside, A. G. (2021). Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA): Guidelines for research practice in information systems and marketing. International Journal of Information Management, 58, Article 102310. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijinfomgt.2021.102310 A practical guide to using fsQCA in information systems and marketing research. It explains the procedure with data from earlier studies and also touches on checking predictive validity and combining fsQCA with methods such as SEM.
Park, Y., Fiss, P. C., & El Sawy, O. A. (2020). Theorizing the multiplicity of digital phenomena: The ecology of configurations, causal recipes, and guidelines for applying QCA. MIS Quarterly, 44(4), 1493-1520. https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2020/13879 For digital phenomena that involve several theoretical perspectives and combinations of conditions, it offers a framework that ties QCA to theory building. Through examples, it explains how to apply QCA to deductive theory testing and to inductive theory building.

title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
text:
4. Choosing the threshold

Krogslund, C., Choi, D. D., & Poertner, M. (2015). Fuzzy sets on shaky ground: Parameter sensitivity and confirmation bias in fsQCA. Political Analysis, 23(1), 21-41. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu016 Argues that fsQCA results can change with small changes in the parameters a user chooses, and that combinations containing randomly generated variables are often found to be sufficient for an outcome. It re-analyzes three existing studies and uses sensitivity analyses and Monte Carlo simulations.

On how the placement of the threshold changes the results, see also Toyoda (2026), Quality & Quantity, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-03092-3.

title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
text: In qualitative comparative analysis (QCA), the thresholds that turn continuous scores into set memberships are usually fixed before the analysis. The resulting solution is then an answer to one specific definition, such as “usage intention is high” meaning a score of 7 or above. ThSQCA is an R package that makes the threshold itself an object of analysis: it repeats the same QCA analysis over a range of thresholds, under identical settings, and records how the sufficiency solution changes.

title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
text:
The idea
Changing a threshold changes which cases belong to a set. That can change the truth table, the fit measures, and the Boolean minimization. The relationship between a threshold t and the sufficiency solution S is therefore better described as a mapping, t → S(t), than as a single solution.
This is not the same question as a robustness check, which asks whether a favored solution survives alternative settings. It is also different from a search for the best threshold. Threshold-sweep QCA asks a descriptive question: how are sufficiency structures distributed across threshold definitions, and where do they persist, appear, or disappear? The methodology is developed in the paper below.

title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
text:
Four sweep functions








Question
Function
Threshold varied




How does the solution change as the target outcome level changes?
otSweep()
Outcome


How does it change as the criterion for one condition changes?
ctSweepS()
One condition


What happens when the criteria for several conditions change together?
ctSweepM()
Several conditions


How does it change when outcome and condition criteria change together?
dtSweep()
Outcome and conditions

title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
text:
Getting started
install.packages("ThSQCA")
library(ThSQCA)
The package includes a small example data set, sample_data, with an outcome Y and three conditions X1, X2, and X3, all scored from 0 to 10. The following is a minimal outcome-threshold sweep that runs as it is:
library(ThSQCA)

head(sample_data)

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = sample_data,
  outcome     = "Y",
  conditions  = c("X1", "X2", "X3"),
  sweep_range = 6:9,
  thrX        = c(X1 = 7, X2 = 7, X3 = 7)
)

summary(res)
This sweep asks how the sufficiency solution changes when “high outcome” is defined as Y >= 6, Y >= 7, Y >= 8, and Y >= 9. Each condition counts as “high” when its score is 7 or above. If you want a slower, step-by-step explanation of every row and of how to read the result table, see part 1 of the beginner’s series.
Running it prints a table like this (only the result part is shown):
 thrY                  expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    6 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.853           1
    7 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.879           1
    8                 No solution    NA    NA           0
    9                 No solution    NA    NA           0
Each row is one outcome threshold. In the expression column, * means AND, + means OR, and ~ means NOT. At Y >= 6 and Y >= 7, the same three sufficient paths appear. At Y >= 8 and Y >= 9, no solution meets the consistency requirement. A single-threshold analysis cannot show where an answer stops holding; a sweep can.
The package vignette covers all four functions with worked examples.

title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
text:
A note on use
ThSQCA is not a device for finding the threshold that gives the most appealing result. The range of thresholds should be justified in advance by the meaning of the scale, theory, and practical goals, and the range explored should be reported in full. The generate_report() function is designed to keep that record.

text: 第2回では、4つのスイープをすべて実行しました。丁寧な分析には、まだ2つの問いが残っています。1つ目は、QCAには3種類の解(複雑解、倹約解、中間解)がありますが、どれを使うべきか、です。2つ目は、1つのセルに最小解が複数あるときは、どうするか、です。この回では、2つ目の、もっと小さな練習用データで、両方に答えます。

title: ThSQCA 入門 第3回: 解の種類と、複数の解
text:
2つ目の練習用データ
企業向けソフトウェアのアカウントを、60件シミュレーションで作ります。各アカウントは、更新スコア(RNW)と、3つの評価をもちます。信頼(TRU)、価格(PRC)、サポート(SUP)で、どれも0〜10点です。この模擬の世界では、信頼が高く、かつ、価格かサポートのどちらかが高いときに、更新が高くなります。3つの評価は強く相関しているので、条件の組み合わせのうち、観察されないものが出てきます。これは意図的です。観察されない組み合わせこそ、3種類の解が、違う扱いをするものだからです。

library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)

Loading required package: admisc



To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.




練習用データ2
make_demo_data2 <- function(n = 60, seed = 89, rho = 0.85) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  L   <- rnorm(n)
  mk  <- function() clip(6 + 2 * (rho * L + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)))
  TRU <- mk(); PRC <- mk(); SUP <- mk()
  RNW <- clip(pmin(TRU, pmax(PRC, SUP)) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(RNW, TRU, PRC, SUP)
}

demo2 <- make_demo_data2()
head(demo2)

2   6   8   7   7
3   9   9   9   7
4   5   5   4   6
5  10  10   8   9
6   1   2   4   5

section: 観察されない組み合わせ(「論理残余」)
text:
観察されない組み合わせ(「論理残余」)
条件が3つあり、それぞれが高いか低いかなら、可能な組み合わせは 2 x 2 x 2 = 8通りです。QCAは、それらを真理表に並べます。QCAパッケージで、真理表を手で作ってみましょう。アウトカムは更新が5以上、各条件の「高い」は7以上とします。

bin2 <- data.frame(
  RNW = as.integer(demo2$RNW >= 5),
  TRU = as.integer(demo2$TRU >= 7),
  PRC = as.integer(demo2$PRC >= 7),
  SUP = as.integer(demo2$SUP >= 7)
)

tt2 <- truthTable(bin2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
tt2


  OUT: output value
    n: number of cases in configuration
 incl: sufficiency inclusion score
  PRI: proportional reduction in inconsistency

    TRU PRC SUP   OUT    n   incl  PRI  
1    0   0   0     0     30  0.433 0.433
2    0   0   1     1     7   0.857 0.857
4    0   1   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
6    1   0   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
7    1   1   0     1     4   1.000 1.000
8    1   1   1     1     13  1.000 1.000


左側の行番号を見てください。可能な8通りのうち、現れるのは6通りだけです(3行目と5行目がありません)。たとえば、信頼だけが高いアカウントや、価格の評価だけが高いアカウントが、データにないからです。欠けている組み合わせが、論理残余です。列 n は、各組み合わせのアカウント数、incl は、それらがどれだけ一貫して更新しているか、OUT は、組み合わせが十分と認められるだけの一貫性があるとき1になります。
残余が重要なのは、Boolean最小化が、式を短くするために、残余を使えるからです。3種類の解は、残余を使うかどうか、どう使うかが違います。

ここで dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1) は、「信頼が高いこと、価格の評価が高いこと、サポートが高いことは、どれも更新に有利だと期待する」という意味です。

text:
3種類の解を並べる
同じアウトカム閾値スイープ(更新が5、6、7、8)を、解の種類だけ変えて、3回実行します。

thr2  <- c(TRU = 7, PRC = 7, SUP = 7)
cond2 <- c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP")

run2 <- function(...) {
  otSweep(dat = demo2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = cond2, sweep_range = 5:8,
          thrX = thr2, incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, ...)
}

res_cx <- run2()                                     # complex
res_ps <- run2(include = "?")                        # parsimonious

Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.

res_im <- run2(include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1))  # intermediate

data.frame(
  thrY         = 5:8,
  complex      = res_cx$summary$expression,
  parsimonious = res_ps$summary$expression,
  intermediate = res_im$summary$expression
)

  thrY            complex   parsimonious       intermediate
1    5      SUP + TRU*PRC      TRU + SUP      SUP + TRU*PRC
2    6 TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP TRU + ~PRC*SUP TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP
3    7            TRU*SUP        TRU*SUP            TRU*SUP
4    8        No solution    No solution        No solution


出力と一緒に表示される警告は、ThSQCAからの注意です。更新が5のとき、倹約解の分析には、同じ長さの解が複数あります。これは、後で扱います。
更新が7のときは、3つとも一致して(TRU*SUP)、8ではどれも解がありません。5と6では、倹約解のほうが短くなります。たとえば、更新が5のとき、倹約解は TRU + SUP ですが、複雑解は SUP + TRU*PRC です。TRU だけの項は、「信頼は高いが、価格とサポートの評価が低い」という組み合わせをカバーしますが、この組み合わせは、データに現れません。倹約解は、この観察されない組み合わせも十分だろう、と仮定する立場です。複雑解は、そのような仮定を置きません。このデータでは、たまたま、中間解は複雑解と一致します。

section: 知っておくべき、ひとつの考え方
text:
知っておくべき、ひとつの考え方
QCAは、あるアウトカムにとって「十分」な条件の組み合わせを探します。顧客ロイヤルティを例にしましょう。「品質が高く、かつサービスが高い」という組み合わせは、それをもつ顧客のほぼ全員が、ロイヤルティも高いなら、ロイヤルティが高いことに十分です。
これを行うために、QCAはまず、「高い」とは誰のことかを決めなければなりません。0〜10点の調査の得点なら、閾値を選びます。得点が閾値以上なら、その変数で「高い」とします。このシリーズでは、得点を閾値で「高い」と「高くない」の2つに分ける、二値(crisp-set)QCA を使います。
ここに落とし穴があります。閾値7も閾値8も、どちらも妥当ですが、答えが変わることがあります。通常のQCA分析は、閾値を1つ選んで、答えを1つ報告します。ThSQCAは、同じ分析を、閾値の範囲全体で繰り返し、すべての答えを1つの表にまとめます。答えが保たれるところと、変わるところが、見えるようになります。
ThSQCAは、QCA パッケージの代わりではありません。閾値ごとに、QCAの truthTable() と minimize() を、毎回同じ設定で呼び出して、結果を集めます。

text:
ステップ2: 小さな練習用データを作る
再現できるように、400人の顧客をシミュレーションで作ります。各顧客は、0〜10点の4つの得点をもちます。ロイヤルティ(LOY)と、品質(QUA)、サービス(SER)、店舗環境(ENV)の評価です。この模擬の世界では、品質とサービスがどちらも高いとき、または、(それより少し弱く)品質と環境がどちらも高いときに、ロイヤルティが高くなります。良い分析なら、これを見つけ出すはずです。

make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()
head(demo)

  LOY QUA SER ENV
1   7   7   9   3
2   5   4   7   5
3   4   6   4   4
4   6   6   6   4
5   5   5   4   7
6   0   1   2   5


1行が、1人の顧客です。上の関数は、理解しなくても構いません。練習用データを作るためだけのものです。自分のデータでは、このような列をもつデータフレームに、ファイルを読み込むだけです。

section: ステップ3: スイープを実行する
text:
ステップ3: スイープを実行する
知りたいのは、「高いロイヤルティ」の基準を上げると、答えがどう変わるか、です。そこで、3つの条件の閾値は7に固定し、アウトカムの閾値を5から8まで動かします。これをアウトカム閾値スイープと呼び、関数は otSweep() です。

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = demo,
  outcome     = "LOY",
  conditions  = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range = 5:8,
  thrX        = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7)
)

各行の意味は、次のとおりです。



引数
意味




dat
分析するデータフレーム


outcome
アウトカムの列


conditions
条件の列


sweep_range
試すアウトカムの閾値。ここでは5、6、7、8


thrX
各条件の固定した閾値。「高い」は7以上



ここに書いていない設定が2つあります。既定値があるためです。組み合わせが十分と認められる最低の一貫性(incl.cut、既定は0.8)と、組み合わせごとの最低の事例数(n.cut、既定は1)です。

section: ステップ4: 結果を読む
text:
ステップ4: 結果を読む

summary(res)

OTS Summary
=========== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: LOY 
  Conditions: QUA, SER, ENV 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 thrY        expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    5 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.981 0.403           1
    6 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.926 0.565           1
    7           QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
    8       No solution    NA    NA           0


表は、アウトカムの閾値ごとに1行です。列は、次のとおりです。

thrY: その行で使ったアウトカムの閾値。1行目では、「高いロイヤルティ」は LOY >= 5 を意味します。
expression: 見つかった十分な組み合わせ。* はAND、+ はOR、~ はNOTです。
inclS: 解の一貫性。解がカバーする事例が、どれだけ確実に、アウトカムの集合に入っているか。高いほどよく、1が完全です。
covS: 解のカバレッジ。アウトカムをもつ事例のうち、解が説明する割合です。
n_solutions: 見つかった、等価な最小解の数(ここでは1)。

では、expression の列を、上から下へ読みましょう。

LOY >= 5 と LOY >= 6 では、2つの組み合わせが十分です。QUA*SER(品質が高く、サービスが高い)と、QUA*ENV(品質が高く、店舗環境が高い)です。
LOY >= 7 では、QUA*SER だけが残ります。
LOY >= 8 では、結果は No solution(解なし)です。この水準では、3つの条件のどの組み合わせも、必要な一貫性に届きませんでした。

これは、シミュレーションに入れておいたとおりの結果で、スイープが役立つ理由も示しています。LOY >= 6 だけを分析していたら、経路が2つあると報告したでしょう。LOY >= 7 だけなら、1つと報告したでしょう。スイープは、答えが、目標がどれだけ高いかに左右されること、そして、どこで通用しなくなるかを、見せてくれます。
「No solution」についての注意です。これは技術的な結果で、高いロイヤルティへの経路が存在しない、という意味ではありません。このデータとこの設定では、QCAが、一貫性の条件を満たす最小解を作れなかった、という意味です。

title: ThSQCA の紹介: Rで閾値スイープQCAを行う
text: 質的比較分析(QCA)では、連続的な得点を集合への所属に変える閾値を、ふつう、分析の前に1つに決めます。そのため、得られる解は、ある1つの定義への答えになります。たとえば、「利用意向が高い」を7点以上と定義したときの答えです。ThSQCA は、閾値そのものを分析の対象にする R パッケージです。同じ QCA の分析を、同じ設定のまま、閾値の範囲全体で繰り返し、十分条件の解がどう変わるかを記録します。

title: ThSQCA の紹介: Rで閾値スイープQCAを行う
text:
考え方
閾値を変えると、どの事例が集合に入るかが変わります。すると、真理表も、適合度の指標も、Boolean最小化の結果も変わることがあります。したがって、閾値 t と十分条件の解 S の関係は、1つの解というより、対応関係 t → S(t) として記述するほうが適切です。
これは、頑健性の確認とは、別の問いです。頑健性の確認は、気に入った解が、別の設定でも残るかを問います。また、最良の閾値を探すことでもありません。閾値スイープQCAは、記述的な問いを立てます。十分条件の構造は、閾値の定義にわたって、どのように分布するのか。どこで持続し、現れ、消えるのか。方法論は、下に挙げる論文で展開しています。

title: ThSQCA の紹介: Rで閾値スイープQCAを行う
section: パッケージが行うこと
text:
パッケージが行うこと
ThSQCA は、独自の最小化アルゴリズムを実装していません。真理表の作成と最小化は、QCA パッケージに任せています。計算の中心は、通常の分析と同じです。ThSQCA が加えるのは、その周りの作業の流れです。

一貫性閾値、頻度閾値、解の種類、方向性の期待を、スイープのすべての段階で同じにします。
項、解の一貫性、カバレッジを、共通の形式にまとめます。
解がない場合や、最小解が複数ある場合も、失わずに記録します。
結果は、表、構成図、軌跡の図、ヒートマップで示せます。Markdown 形式のレポートとしても書き出せます。

title: ThSQCA の紹介: Rで閾値スイープQCAを行う
text:
はじめてみる
install.packages("ThSQCA")
library(ThSQCA)
パッケージには、小さな例のデータ sample_data が入っています。アウトカム Y と、3つの条件 X1、X2、X3 で、どれも0〜10点です。次は、そのまま動く、最小のアウトカム閾値スイープです。
library(ThSQCA)

head(sample_data)

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = sample_data,
  outcome     = "Y",
  conditions  = c("X1", "X2", "X3"),
  sweep_range = 6:9,
  thrX        = c(X1 = 7, X2 = 7, X3 = 7)
)

summary(res)
このスイープは、「高いアウトカム」を Y >= 6、Y >= 7、Y >= 8、Y >= 9 と定義したときに、十分条件の解がどう変わるかを調べます。各条件は、得点が7以上のとき「高い」とします。各行の意味や、結果の表の読み方を、ゆっくり、順を追って知りたい方は、入門シリーズの第1回をご覧ください。
実行すると、次のような表が出ます(結果の部分だけを示します)。
 thrY                  expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    6 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.853           1
    7 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.879           1
    8                 No solution    NA    NA           0
    9                 No solution    NA    NA           0
1行が、1つのアウトカム閾値です。expression の列では、* が AND、+ が OR、~ が NOT を表します。Y >= 6 と Y >= 7 では、同じ3つの十分な経路が現れます。Y >= 8 と Y >= 9 では、一貫性の条件を満たす解がありません。閾値を1つにした分析だけでは、答えがどこで成り立たなくなるかは見えません。スイープなら、それが見えます。
パッケージのビネットには、4つの関数すべてについて、実例つきの説明があります。

title: ThSQCA の紹介: Rで閾値スイープQCAを行う
text:
使うときの注意
ThSQCA は、いちばん魅力的な結果を出す閾値を探すための道具ではありません。閾値の範囲は、尺度の意味、理論、実務上の目標に基づいて、あらかじめ正当化しておく必要があります。探索した範囲は、すべて報告してください。generate_report() 関数は、その記録を残すために作られています。

text:
Short definitions, in plain language. Each is a first step, not a full treatment.

QCA (qualitative comparative analysis)

A method that looks for combinations of conditions that go with an outcome, using set relations rather than averages.

Condition and outcome

A condition is a possible cause (for example, high quality). The outcome is what you want to explain (for example, loyalty).

Crisp set and fuzzy set

In a crisp set, each case is in or out (0 or 1). In a fuzzy set, each case has a degree of membership between 0 and 1.

Calibration

Turning raw scores into set membership scores, using chosen thresholds for “fully in”, “fully out”, and the crossover point.

Truth table

A table with one row for each combination of conditions, showing how many cases fall in that row and how consistently they show the outcome.

Necessity and sufficiency

A condition is necessary if the outcome is not found without it. A condition (or combination) is sufficient if the outcome is found whenever it is present.

Consistency (inclS) and coverage (covS)

Consistency shows how well the cases follow a sufficiency relation. Coverage shows how much of the outcome the relation accounts for.

PRI

A measure that helps detect a condition combination that looks sufficient for both the outcome and its absence.

Configuration (recipe)

A combination of conditions that together are linked to the outcome.

Equifinality

More than one configuration can lead to the same outcome.

Asymmetry

The causes of the outcome’s presence need not be the mirror image of the causes of its absence.

Minimization and solution

The step that simplifies the truth table into shorter expressions. The result is called the solution.

Threshold sweep

Rerunning the same analysis across a range of thresholds, under identical settings, and recording how the solutions change.

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
text:
前回は、なぜ QCA が意思決定に向くのかを説明しました。最後に残った疑問は、「高い」を分ける基準をどこに置くか、です。今回は、その問題に取り組みます。
同じ会社の2人のマネージャーが、同じ顧客調査を見ています。
1人目は顧客層を広げたいと考えています。ブランドを「使ってもよい」と思う人を、できるだけ増やしたいのです。2人目はファンを育てたいと考えています。「ぜひ使いたい」と心から思う顧客を、つくりたいのです。2人とも、同じ問いを立てます。「顧客をそこに連れていくには、ブランドのどんな強みを組み合わせればよいのか」。
ここに、困った点があります。標準的な分析は、この問いに1つの基準でしか答えを出しません。「高い」を7点以上と決めれば、答えは1つです。8点にしていたら、別の答えになったかもしれません。複数の基準にわたる結果が、体系的に報告されるとは限りません。そのため、ファンを育てたい人と、顧客層を広げたい人が、同じ施策をとるべきなのかどうかは、1つの基準の分析だけでは分かりません。

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
section: 基準は、変えてみるもの
text:
基準は、変えてみるもの
閾値スイープ QCA(ThSQCA)は、基準を1つに決めず、変えて試します。ほかの条件をすべて同じにして、同じ分析をいくつかの基準で実行し、答えを1つの表に並べます。答えが安定しているところ、形が変わるところ、消えてしまうところが、見えるようになります。
トップボックスとトップ2ボックスの集計をしたことがある方は、この問題をご存じのはずです。トップ2ボックスでは確かな結果に見えても、トップボックスでは、まったく違って見えることがあります。スイープは、この比較を、体系的に行います。

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
text:
小さな例(模擬データ)
実際の顧客データを使わずに考え方を示すため、あるカフェブランドの顧客400人を、シミュレーションで作りました。顧客はそれぞれ、ブランドの品質、サービス、店舗環境を0〜10点で評価し、ロイヤルティも0〜10点で答えています。ここでは、得点を「7点以上か、そうでないか」の2つに分ける、二値(crisp-set)QCA の例で説明します。次のように問います。「高い」評価(7点以上)をどう組み合わせれば、顧客は、それぞれのロイヤルティの目標に届くのか。

基準が上がるにつれて、表を下に読んでください。

ほどほどの目標には、選択肢があります。 経路は2つあるので、マネージャーは、費用の少ない方を選べます。品質とサービスを高めるか、品質と店舗を高めるか、です。
厳しい目標には、選択肢が少なくなります。 7点以上では、品質とサービスの経路だけが残ります。店舗環境は、入口ではなくなります。
非常に厳しい目標は、データの説明力を超えることがあります。 8点以上では、3つの強みの、単独でも組み合わせでも、足りませんでした。これは、経路が存在しない証拠ではありません。この3つの強みでは、最上位の顧客を説明できない、ということです。追加の条件、測定、事例数、分析設定を再検討する手がかりになります。

「7点以上」だけの分析では、1人目のマネージャーに、誤解を招く答えを伝えてしまいます。品質とサービスが唯一の経路だと言ってしまうのですが、広い目標では、もう1つの経路があるのです。

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
section: どんな問いに役立つか
text:
どんな問いに役立つか

満足度、推奨意向(NPSの質問項目など)、購入意向: 「満足」のレシピは、「感動」のレシピと同じでしょうか。
セグメントの定義: 「ヘビーユーザー」を年10回購入とするか、20回とするかで、要因は変わるでしょうか。
キャンペーンの目標: 顧客を「検討する」から「選ぶ」へ動かすには、何が必要でしょうか。
報告: 1つの基準を弁護する代わりに、範囲を見せて、答えが基準にどれだけ左右されるかを、読み手に示せます。

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
text:
2つの正直な注意点

結果は、成果と一緒に現れる強みの組み合わせを示します。 観察データの分析に共通して、因果関係の証明にはなりません。どこを見るか、何を検証するかを決めるための地図として使ってください。
いちばん都合のよい答えが出る基準を、探さないでください。 結果を見る前に範囲を決めて、理由を説明し、すべてを報告します。スイープの価値は、答えが定義にどれだけ依存するかを、透明にすることにあります。

title: 「ほどほど」と「大好き」は、同じ目標でしょうか。マーケターのための閾値スイープ QCA
text:
自分の調査で試す
ゼロからコードを書く必要はありません。

QCA Quickstart が、手元のデータの列名から、最初の分析スクリプトを作ります。
Sweep Builder が、その設定を、閾値スイープのスクリプトに変換します。
スクリプトを R に貼り付けます。パッケージは無料です(install.packages("ThSQCA"))。

同じ考え方を、もう少しゆっくり学びたい方には、初心者向けシリーズがあります。練習用データを使って、1行ずつ説明しています。手法そのものは、Toyoda (2026) の論文「Threshold-sweep QCA: threshold dependence as an analytical dimension」(Quality & Quantity)で解説しています。パッケージは CRAN にあります。

title: QCA を知るための論文と本: 最初に読む 6 点(基礎編)
text: 前回までは、QCA が意思決定に向く理由と、基準の置き方を説明しました。ここでは、QCA を学ぶときに、分野を問わず最初に読まれる標準的な文献を、目的別に紹介します。

title: QCA を知るための論文と本: 最初に読む 6 点(基礎編)
text:
1. 考え方と測り方(論文)

Mahoney, J., & Goertz, G. (2006). A tale of two cultures: Contrasting quantitative and qualitative research. Political Analysis, 14(3), 227-249. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj017 量的研究と質的研究を、価値観、信念、規範の異なる「2つの文化」として対比し、説明、因果、事例の選び方、測定など、10の側面から比べています。QCA がどのような研究の伝統に立っているかを知る出発点になります。
Ragin, C. C. (2006). Set relations in social research: Evaluating their consistency and coverage. Political Analysis, 14(3), 291-310. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj019 集合の関係を評価する2つの指標、一貫性(consistency)とカバレッジ(coverage)を紹介した論文です。ファジィ集合を使うことで、二値の変数や誤差の扱いに関するそれまでの制約を乗り越えられることを示しています。
Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2010). Standards of good practice in qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) and fuzzy-sets. Comparative Sociology, 9(3), 397-418. https://doi.org/10.1163/156913210X12493538729793 QCA とファジィ集合を用いるときの、標準的な良い実践(good practice)を整理した論文です。分析を始める前に、守るべき手続きを確認するのに役立ちます。

title: QCA を知るための論文と本: 最初に読む 6 点(基礎編)
section: 2. 手法を体系的に学ぶ(本)
text:
2. 手法を体系的に学ぶ(本)

Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press. 集合論的な分析と従来の量的研究を対比しながら、キャリブレーション、条件の組み合わせ、因果の複雑さを解説しています。QCA の手順だけでなく、その背後にある研究の考え方を学ぶための本です。
Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2012). Set-Theoretic Methods for the Social Sciences: A Guide to Qualitative Comparative Analysis. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139004244 集合論の基礎から QCA の実践までを、体系的に解説した教科書です。分析上の注意点や陥りやすい問題も扱い、手順と判断の根拠をあわせて理解するのに役立ちます。
Oana, I.-E., Schneider, C. Q., & Thomann, E. (2021). Qualitative Comparative Analysis Using R: A Beginner’s Guide. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009006781 QCA を R で行うための、初学者向けの入門書です。R で分析を進めたい読者が、基本の操作を確認するのに向いています。

次の記事では、マーケティング・経営学で QCA を使った論文と、経営・組織研究での理論的な背景(応用編)を紹介します。

準備: 第1回と同じ練習用データ

library(ThSQCA)



練習用データ(第1回と同じ)
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()


データの背景を思い出してください。品質(QUA)とサービス(SER)がどちらも高いとき、または、それより少し弱く、品質と店舗環境(ENV)がどちらも高いときに、ロイヤルティ(LOY)が高くなります。

section: スイープ1: ctSweepS() で、1つの条件を動かす
text:
スイープ1: ctSweepS() で、1つの条件を動かす
「サービスが高い」の線をどこに引くか、迷っているとします。6で十分でしょうか。7でしょうか。9でしょうか。アウトカムを LOY >= 7 に固定し、ほかの条件を7に固定して、SER の閾値を5から9まで動かします。

res_cts <- ctSweepS(
  dat          = demo,
  outcome      = "LOY",
  conditions   = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_var    = "SER",
  sweep_range  = 5:9,
  thrY         = 7,
  thrX_default = 7
)

summary(res_cts)

CTS (single) Summary
==================== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: LOY 
  Conditions: QUA, SER, ENV 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 threshold   expression inclS  covS n_solutions
         5  No solution    NA    NA           0
         6  No solution    NA    NA           0
         7      QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
         8      QUA*SER 0.909 0.333           1
         9 QUA*SER*~ENV 0.917 0.122           1


新しい引数は、sweep_var(閾値を動かす条件)、thrY(固定するアウトカムの閾値)、thrX_default(ほかのすべての条件の、固定する閾値)です。
表を上から下へ読みます。「サービスが高い」を5または6と定義すると、解はありません。定義がゆるすぎて、「サービスを十分に受けた」顧客の集団が、もはや確実にはロイヤルではなくなるからです。7と8では、解は QUA*SER です。9では、解に3つ目の要素が加わって QUA*SER*~ENV になり、カバレッジは、7での0.656から、9での0.122へと、大きく下がります。いちばん厳しい定義の背後に、顧客が何人いるかを数えると、理由が分かります。

sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9)                 # 品質とサービスの両方が高い顧客

[1] 16

sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9 & demo$ENV < 7)  # 解 QUA*SER*~ENV を満たす顧客

[1] 12


その水準で、品質とサービスの両方が高い顧客は、400人のうち16人です。そのうち、店舗環境が7未満で、解 QUA*SER*~ENV を満たす顧客は、12人だけです。そこでの結果は、ごく少数の事例に支えられています。これは役に立つ習慣です。解が格子の端にしか現れないときは、その背後にある事例の数を確かめてください。

title: ThSQCA 入門 第2回: 4つのスイープと、範囲の決め方
section: 擁護できる範囲を選ぶ
text:
擁護できる範囲を選ぶ
スイープは、簡単に実行できます。だからこそ、規律が必要です。たくさんの閾値を試して、都合のよいものだけを報告すれば、研究者の自由度を減らすどころか、増やしてしまいます。目安を挙げます。

結果を見る前に、範囲を決める。 尺度の意味、理論、実務上の目標(たとえば「許容できる」「良い」「とても良い」)に基づいて決めます。
基準点を含める。 通常の分析で使う閾値は、格子の中に入れておきます。読み手が比較できるようにするためです。
中立の領域を避ける。 0〜10の尺度では、中点のあたりの得点は、誰にとっても、はっきり「高い」とは言えません。そのため、範囲は、たいてい、それより上から始めます。
読める大きさに、格子を抑える。 変数ごとに、意味のある値を少し選ぶほうが、可能な値をすべて並べるより、よいです。
端の事例数を確かめる。 格子の端のセルは、ごく少数の事例に支えられていることが、よくあります。
格子全体を報告する。 ストーリーに合うセルだけでなく、安定した領域も、不安定な領域も、示します。

text:
最初の3回では、スイープを実行して、読み方を学びました。最終回では、スイープを、報告でき、擁護できる形にします。何を探索したかの記録、構成図、そして、数値がQCAパッケージと一致することの確認です。
library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)

Loading required package: admisc



To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.
練習用データ(第1回と同じ)
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()
第1回のアウトカム閾値スイープを、再び使います。今回は、レポートに必要な、完全な詳細を求めます。
res_ots <- otSweep(
  dat            = demo,
  outcome        = "LOY",
  conditions     = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range    = 5:8,
  thrX           = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7),
  incl.cut       = 0.8,
  n.cut          = 1,
  return_details = TRUE
)

スイープ全体を記録するレポート
スイープは、たくさんの結果を作ります。読み手は、どの範囲を、どの設定で探索し、閾値ごとに何が出たかを、知る必要があります。generate_report() は、それをMarkdownファイルに書き出します。形式は2つあります。

"simple" は、本文や付録のための、短いレポートです。要約の表、閾値ごとの解、QCAパッケージで結果を確かめるためのコードが入ります。
"full" は、補足資料のためのものです。分析の概要(スイープの範囲と基準値)、記述統計に加えて、閾値ごとに、真理表、解の適合度、項ごとの指標、構成図、QCAパッケージの出力、再現に必要な設定が入ります。そのあとに、閾値どうしの比較が続きます。


report_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
generate_report(res_ots, report_file, dat = demo, format = "simple")

QCAパッケージで、セルを確認する
ThSQCAは、新しい結果を作り出すわけではありません。どのセルも、普通のQCA分析なので、どのセルでも、手で再現できます。これは、道具への信頼を築く、よい方法で、査読者に聞かれたときの答えにもなります。ここでは、アウトカム閾値が7のセルを再現します。

bin <- function(x, t) as.integer(x >= t)

d7 <- data.frame(
  LOY = bin(demo$LOY, 7), QUA = bin(demo$QUA, 7),
  SER = bin(demo$SER, 7), ENV = bin(demo$ENV, 7)
)

tt  <- truthTable(d7, outcome = "LOY", conditions = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
sol <- minimize(tt)
sol


M1: QUA*SER -> LOY


minimize() が出力した解は、第1回のスイープ表の thrY = 7 の行(QUA*SER)と一致します。どちらも、データを同じ方法で二値化し(得点が7以上なら、集合に入る)、どちらも、同じQCAの関数が最小化を行ったからです。

title: なぜ QCA は意思決定に向くのか: 「単独の効果」ではなく「レシピ」を探す分析
text:
マーケティング・マネージャーの問いは、「品質を上げれば、顧客は増えるか」だけではありません。多くの場合は、「何と何を組み合わせれば、目標に届くのか」です。
質的比較分析(QCA)は、この問いに答えるために作られた分析です。回帰分析のような統計手法は、他の条件を一定にしたとき、1つの要因が単独でどれだけ効くかを見るのが得意です。QCA は、別の角度から、データを見ます。

title: なぜ QCA は意思決定に向くのか: 「単独の効果」ではなく「レシピ」を探す分析
section: 意思決定にとって魅力的な理由
text:
意思決定にとって魅力的な理由

1. 施策は、単独ではなく組み合わせで動かす
店舗の改装、接客の強化、価格の見直しは、たいてい一緒に実行されます。QCA は、「品質が高く、かつサービスが高い」のように、条件の組み合わせ(レシピ)を単位に、結果を見ます。


2. 成功への経路は、1つとは限らない
同じ成果に、複数の経路があることがあります(等結果性)。QCA は、選んだ条件と分析設定のもとで、成果に結びつく複数の経路を特定できます。経営者は、予算や強みに合わせて、どの経路が自社に合うかを選べます。


3. 成功の理由は、失敗の理由の裏返しとは限らない
ロイヤルティが高い顧客を生む条件と、離反する顧客を生む条件は、別の分析が必要なことがあります(非対称性)。QCA は、高い場合と低い場合を、別々に分析します。


4. 小〜中規模の事例でも、使える
店舗、ブランド、キャンペーン、法人顧客のように、事例が数十から数百の単位でも、事例の中身を見ながら分析できます。小〜中規模の事例比較にも使えます。ただし、条件の数に対して事例が少ないと、論理残余(データにない条件の組み合わせ)が多くなります。


5. 結果が「もし〜なら」の形で読める
結果は、「品質が高く、かつサービスが高い」という、短い規則として出ます。会議で説明しやすく、現場でも、何をすればよいかが伝わります。


6. 「必須」と「十分」を区別できる
「これがなければ成功しない」(必要条件)と、「これがあれば成功する」(十分条件)を、区別して扱えます。「外せない施策」と「勝ち筋」を、分けて考えられます。

section: QCA にできないこと(と、他の分析にも言えること)
text:
QCA にできないこと(と、他の分析にも言えること)

因果関係を、QCA だけが証明できないわけではありません。 観察データの分析は、回帰分析を含めて、因果関係を証明しきれません。QCA で得られた十分条件の解だけから、施策を実施した場合の因果効果が保証されるわけではありません。因果的に解釈するには、研究設計、時間的順序、理論、事例知識などによる裏づけが必要です。結果は、施策候補や検証すべき仮説を考える材料として活用できます。
理論と事例の知識が必要です。 条件の選び方や、どこから「高い」とするかは、分析する人が決めます。

title: なぜ QCA は意思決定に向くのか: 「単独の効果」ではなく「レシピ」を探す分析
section: 落とし穴は、「基準」にある
text:
落とし穴は、「基準」にある
最後の点が、実は重要です。QCA では、「高い」と「低い」を分ける基準(閾値)を、分析する人が決めます。ところが、意思決定の目標とは、まさにこの基準のことです。「ほどほどに満足」を目指すのか、「大好き」を目指すのか。基準を変えると、答えも変わることがあります。
この問題には、閾値スイープ QCA(ThSQCA)で取り組みます。続きは、次の記事です。

title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
text:
The previous post explained why QCA suits decision-making. One question was left open: where should the line between “high” and “low” go? This post takes it up.
Two managers in the same company are looking at the same customer survey.
The first wants to widen the base: get as many customers as possible to say the brand is acceptable to use. The second wants to build fans: create customers who really want to use the brand. Both ask the same question: “What combination of brand strengths gets customers there?”
Here is the uncomfortable part. A standard analysis answers that question for one cutoff. If you define “high” as a score of 7 or above, you get one answer. If you had chosen 8, you might have gotten a different one. Results across several cutoffs are not always reported systematically, so a single analysis cannot tell us whether the manager who wants fans and the manager who wants a wider base should be doing the same thing.

title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
section: The cutoff is something to vary
text:
The cutoff is something to vary
Threshold-sweep QCA (ThSQCA) does not fix the cutoff in advance. It tries several. You run the same analysis at several cutoffs, with everything else held constant, and line the answers up in one table. You see where the answer holds steady, where it changes shape, and where it disappears.
If you have used top-box versus top-2-box scoring, you already know the problem. A result that looks solid at top-2-box can look very different at top-box. The sweep makes that comparison systematic.

title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
text:
A small example (simulated data)
To show the idea without using real customer data, we simulated 400 customers of a café brand. Each customer rated the brand from 0 to 10 on quality, service, and store environment, and also gave a loyalty score from 0 to 10. To keep things simple, we treat each rating as a yes/no split at 7 (crisp-set QCA). We then asked: which combinations of “high” ratings (7 or above) are enough for customers to reach each loyalty target?

Read down the table as the bar rises.

A modest goal has options. There are two routes, so a manager can choose the cheaper one: improve quality and service, or improve quality and the store.
A demanding goal has fewer options. At 7 or above, only the quality and service route remains. The store environment stops being a way in.
A very demanding goal can outrun the data. At 8 or above, none of the three strengths, alone or in combination, was enough. That is not proof that no route exists; it tells you that these three strengths do not explain the very top. It is a cue to revisit additional conditions, measurement, the number of cases, and the analysis settings.

A single analysis at “7 or above” would have told the first manager something misleading: that quality and service is the only route, when for a broader goal there is a second one.

title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
text:
Questions where this helps

Satisfaction, recommendation intent (such as the NPS question), or purchase intent: does the recipe for “satisfied” equal the recipe for “delighted”?
Segment definitions: if “heavy user” means 10 purchases a year versus 20, do the drivers change?
Campaign targets: what does it take to move customers from “consider” to “prefer”?
Reporting: instead of defending one cutoff, show the range and let readers see how much depends on it.

title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
text:
Two honest cautions

It shows combinations that go together with the outcome. It does not prove cause. This is true of any analysis of observational data. Treat the results as a map for where to look and what to test.
Do not hunt for the cutoff that gives the nicest answer. Decide the range before you look, say why, and report all of it. The value of the sweep is in being transparent about how much the answer depends on the definition.

section: Try it on your own survey
text:
Try it on your own survey
You do not need to write code from scratch.

QCA Quickstart creates a first analysis script from the names of your columns.
Sweep Builder turns that setup into a threshold-sweep script.
Paste the script into R. The package is free: install.packages("ThSQCA").

If you would like a gentler walk through the same ideas, the beginner’s series explains every line with a practice data set. The method itself is described in Toyoda (2026), Threshold-sweep QCA: threshold dependence as an analytical dimension, Quality & Quantity, and the package is on CRAN.

title: Papers and books for getting to know QCA: six to read first (basics)
text:
The earlier posts explained why QCA suits decision-making and why the placement of the threshold matters. Here is a short list of the standard readings that people in any field tend to start with when they learn QCA, grouped by purpose.
The summaries below stay within what the publishers’ abstracts and descriptions say. They are not evaluations based on a full reading.

title: Papers and books for getting to know QCA: six to read first (basics)
section: 1. Getting the idea and the measures (papers)
text:
1. Getting the idea and the measures (papers)

Mahoney, J., & Goertz, G. (2006). A tale of two cultures: Contrasting quantitative and qualitative research. Political Analysis, 14(3), 227-249. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj017 Contrasts quantitative and qualitative research as two cultures with different values, beliefs, and norms, and compares them across ten dimensions, including explanation, causation, case selection, and measurement. A starting point for seeing which research tradition QCA belongs to.
Ragin, C. C. (2006). Set relations in social research: Evaluating their consistency and coverage. Political Analysis, 14(3), 291-310. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj019 Introduces two measures for evaluating set relations, consistency and coverage. It shows that fuzzy sets overcome earlier limits on binary variables and on tolerance for error.
Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2010). Standards of good practice in qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) and fuzzy-sets. Comparative Sociology, 9(3), 397-418. https://doi.org/10.1163/156913210X12493538729793 Sets out standards of good practice for QCA and fuzzy sets. Useful for checking the procedures to follow before you start an analysis.

title: Papers and books for getting to know QCA: six to read first (basics)
text:
2. Learning the method systematically (books)

Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press. Contrasts set-theoretic analysis with conventional quantitative research and explains calibration, combinations of conditions, and causal complexity. A book for learning the way of thinking behind QCA, not only its procedure.
Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2012). Set-Theoretic Methods for the Social Sciences: A Guide to Qualitative Comparative Analysis. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139004244 A textbook that runs from the basics of set theory to the practice of QCA. It also covers cautions and common problems, which helps you understand the procedure together with the reasons behind each judgment.
Oana, I.-E., Schneider, C. Q., & Thomann, E. (2021). Qualitative Comparative Analysis Using R: A Beginner’s Guide. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009006781 A beginner’s guide to running QCA in R. A good fit for readers who want to carry out the analysis in R and check the basic operations.

The next post introduces papers that use QCA in marketing and management, together with the theoretical background from management and organization research (applications).

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
text: In part 1 we ran an outcome threshold sweep and read its result. ThSQCA has four sweep functions in total. This post runs all four on the same practice data, and ends with practical advice on choosing the range of thresholds.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
section: The four sweeps at a glance

The four sweeps at a glance

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
section: Setup: the same practice data as part 1
text:
Setup: the same practice data as part 1

library(ThSQCA)



Practice data (identical to part 1)
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()


Remember the story behind the data: loyalty (LOY) is high when quality (QUA) and service (SER) are both high, or, a little less strongly, when quality and the store environment (ENV) are both high.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
text:
Sweep 1: one condition with ctSweepS()
Suppose you are unsure where to draw the line for “high service delivery”. Is 6 high enough? 7? 9? Fix the outcome at LOY >= 7, fix the other conditions at 7, and sweep the threshold of SER from 5 to 9.

res_cts <- ctSweepS(
  dat          = demo,
  outcome      = "LOY",
  conditions   = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_var    = "SER",
  sweep_range  = 5:9,
  thrY         = 7,
  thrX_default = 7
)

summary(res_cts)

CTS (single) Summary
==================== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: LOY 
  Conditions: QUA, SER, ENV 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 threshold   expression inclS  covS n_solutions
         5  No solution    NA    NA           0
         6  No solution    NA    NA           0
         7      QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
         8      QUA*SER 0.909 0.333           1
         9 QUA*SER*~ENV 0.917 0.122           1


The new arguments are sweep_var (the condition whose threshold is swept), thrY (the fixed outcome threshold), and thrX_default (the fixed threshold for all other conditions).
Reading the table from top to bottom: when “high service” is defined as 5 or 6, there is no solution, because the definition is so loose that the group of “highly served” customers is no longer reliably loyal. At 7 and 8 the solution is QUA*SER. At 9 the solution gains a third element, QUA*SER*~ENV, and coverage falls sharply, from 0.656 at 7 to 0.122 at 9. You can see why by counting how many customers are behind the strictest definition:

sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9)                 # customers high on both quality and service

[1] 16

sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9 & demo$ENV < 7)  # customers satisfying the solution QUA*SER*~ENV

[1] 12


Of the 400 customers, 16 are high on both quality and service, and only 12 of them also have a store-environment score below 7, which is what the solution QUA*SER*~ENV requires. The result there rests on very few cases. This is a useful habit: when a solution appears only at the edge of the grid, check how many cases are behind it.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
text:
Sweep 2: several conditions with ctSweepM()
Now let the thresholds of all three conditions vary at once: each of QUA, SER, and ENV is tried at 6, 7, and 8. That is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 combinations. The outcome stays at LOY >= 7.

res_mcts <- ctSweepM(
  dat        = demo,
  outcome    = "LOY",
  conditions = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_list = list(QUA = 6:8, SER = 6:8, ENV = 6:8),
  thrY       = 7
)

Some patterns to look for:

Fourteen of the 27 combinations have a solution. In every combination where “high quality” is defined as 6, there is no solution at all.
With QUA at 7 and SER at 7 or 8, the solution is QUA*SER no matter which threshold is used for ENV. This is a stable region.
With QUA at 8, the solution depends on ENV (and on SER). With ENV at 6 it is QUA*SER (when SER is 7 or 8). With ENV at 7 it is QUA*SER*~ENV. With ENV at 8 it varies, from QUA*ENV alone to two-path solutions such as QUA*SER + QUA*ENV. When “high quality” is defined strictly, the definition of the store environment starts to matter.

The grid shows both where a conclusion is robust and where it is fragile, which a single analysis cannot.

At LOY >= 7, only two definitions still give a solution, the ones where QUA and SER are both at 7. At LOY >= 8, none do. In this data set, raising the target level is the strongest driver of change.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
section: Choosing a range you can defend
text:
Choosing a range you can defend
A sweep is easy to run, which is exactly why it needs discipline. Trying many thresholds and reporting only the convenient ones would add researcher degrees of freedom instead of removing them. Some rules of thumb:

Decide the range before you look at the results. Base it on what the scale means, on theory, and on practical targets (for example “acceptable”, “good”, “very good”).
Include your baseline. The threshold you would have used in an ordinary analysis should be inside the grid, so readers can compare.
Avoid the neutral zone. On a 0 to 10 scale, scores around the midpoint do not clearly mean “high” for anyone, so ranges usually start above it.
Keep the grid small enough to read. A few meaningful values per variable are better than every possible value.
Check the case counts at the edges. Cells at the extremes of the grid often rest on very few cases.
Report the whole grid. Show the stable and the unstable regions, not only the cells that support your story.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 4: reporting and checking your results
text:
In the first three parts we ran sweeps and learned to read them. In this last part we turn a sweep into something you can report and defend: a written record of what was explored, a chart of the configurations, and a check that the numbers agree with the QCA package.
library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)

Loading required package: admisc



To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.
Practice data (identical to part 1)
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()
We reuse the outcome threshold sweep from part 1. This time we ask for the full details, which the report needs.
res_ots <- otSweep(
  dat            = demo,
  outcome        = "LOY",
  conditions     = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range    = 5:8,
  thrX           = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7),
  incl.cut       = 0.8,
  n.cut          = 1,
  return_details = TRUE
)

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 4: reporting and checking your results
section: A report that records the whole sweep
text:
A report that records the whole sweep
A sweep produces many results, and a reader needs to know what range was explored, under which settings, and what came out at each threshold. generate_report() writes this into a Markdown file. It comes in two formats.

"simple" is a short report for the main text or an appendix. It has a summary table, the solution at each threshold, and code for checking the result with the QCA package.
"full" is for supplementary material. It adds an overview of the analysis (the sweep range and the cutoffs), descriptive statistics, and, for every threshold, the truth table, the solution fit, per-term metrics, a configuration chart, the QCA package output, and the settings needed to reproduce it. A comparison across thresholds follows.


report_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
generate_report(res_ots, report_file, dat = demo, format = "simple")

Here are the first lines of the file it wrote. On your own computer, give the file a real name, such as "ots_report_simple.md", and it will appear in your working folder.

cat(head(readLines(report_file), 25), sep = "\n")

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 4: reporting and checking your results
section: Check a cell against the QCA package
text:
Check a cell against the QCA package
ThSQCA does not invent new results. Every cell is an ordinary QCA analysis, so you can reproduce any cell by hand. This is a good way to build trust in the tool, and to answer a reviewer who asks. Here we reproduce the cell at an outcome threshold of 7.

bin <- function(x, t) as.integer(x >= t)

d7 <- data.frame(
  LOY = bin(demo$LOY, 7), QUA = bin(demo$QUA, 7),
  SER = bin(demo$SER, 7), ENV = bin(demo$ENV, 7)
)

tt  <- truthTable(d7, outcome = "LOY", conditions = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
sol <- minimize(tt)
sol


M1: QUA*SER -> LOY


The solution printed by minimize() matches the row for thrY = 7 in the sweep table from part 1 (QUA*SER). In both cases the data were binarized in the same way (a score of 7 or above is a member), and in both cases the same QCA functions did the minimization.

title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 4: reporting and checking your results
section: A short checklist for reporting a sweep
text:
A short checklist for reporting a sweep
Because a sweep gives you freedom to explore, it also asks you to be transparent. Before you report one, make sure that you can answer yes to each of these questions.

Did I decide the threshold range, and the step between values, before looking at the results?
Do I state every setting that was held fixed (consistency cutoff, frequency cutoff, solution type, directional expectations)?
Did I report every cell of the grid, including the cells with no solution?
Did I check how many cases stand behind the cells at the edges of the grid?
If a cell had several minimal solutions, did I say so?
Did I avoid presenting the sweep as a search for the best threshold?
Did I record the versions of R, QCA, and ThSQCA?

title: Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects
text:
A marketing manager’s question is not only “If we raise quality, will customers increase?” More often it is “Which things should we combine to reach our target?”
Qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) was built to answer that kind of question. Statistical methods such as regression are good at showing how much one factor matters on its own, with the other conditions held constant. QCA looks at the data from a different angle.

title: Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects
section: Why QCA is attractive for decisions
text:
Why QCA is attractive for decisions

1. Actions are taken in combination, not alone
Store renovation, better service, and a price review are usually carried out together. QCA takes the combination (the recipe) as its unit, for example “high quality and high service”, and asks what happens to the outcome.


2. There may be more than one road to success
The same outcome can be reached in several ways (equifinality). Under the conditions and analysis settings you choose, QCA can identify several routes to the same outcome, so a manager can choose the one that fits the budget and the company’s strengths.


3. The reasons for success are not always the mirror image of the reasons for failure
The conditions that produce loyal customers and the conditions that produce customers who leave may need separate analyses (asymmetry). QCA analyzes the high case and the low case separately.


4. It can be used with small to medium numbers of cases
With stores, brands, campaigns, or corporate customers, you may have only dozens or a few hundred cases. QCA lets you analyze them while keeping an eye on what is inside each case, It can be used for small to medium comparative case sets. When there are few cases relative to the number of conditions, however, many logical remainders arise (combinations of conditions that no case shows).


5. The result reads as an “if … then” rule
A result comes out as a short rule, such as “high quality and high service”. It is easy to explain in a meeting, and it tells people on the front line what to do.


6. It separates “necessary” from “sufficient”
You can treat “without this, success does not happen” (a necessary condition) differently from “with this, success happens” (a sufficient condition). That lets you think separately about the actions you cannot skip and the actions that win.

title: Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects
section: What QCA cannot do (and what is also true of other methods)
text:
What QCA cannot do (and what is also true of other methods)

QCA is not the only method that cannot prove causation. Analyses of observational data, regression included, cannot fully establish causation. A sufficiency solution from QCA does not, by itself, guarantee the causal effect of carrying out an intervention. A causal reading needs support from research design, temporal order, theory, and case knowledge. The results are best used as material for thinking about candidate interventions and hypotheses to test.
It needs theory and knowledge of the cases. The analyst decides which conditions to include and where “high” begins.

title: Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects
text:
The pitfall is the threshold
That last point matters more than it first appears. In QCA, the analyst decides the threshold that separates “high” from “low”. But a decision target is exactly such a threshold: do you aim for “reasonably satisfied” or for “loved”? When the threshold changes, the answer can change too.
Threshold-sweep QCA (ThSQCA) addresses this problem. The next post continues from here.
